981.quote_or_event: “One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has - O Nanak, he knows the Path.”
981.explanation: Guru Nanak sums up the Sikh way of life in two ordinary habits, kirat karni (living by honest work) and vand chhakna (sharing what one earns). The person who does both as a matter of course is the one who knows the Path.
981.tie_back: The Kural says that for those who know what is due from them every good act is simply duty done as a matter of course, and Guru Nanak likewise finds the true path in goodness made into an everyday habit.
981.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Sarang, Vaar Sarang, Salok Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
981._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); a reasonable but partial fit, since the salok names specific duties (work and sharing) rather than the Kural's general idea of goodness as natural duty for the perfected.

982.quote_or_event: “Truth is higher than everything; but higher still is truthful living.”
982.explanation: Guru Nanak puts lived conduct (sach aachaar) above every other attainment, even above truth held only as an idea. In the Sikh view character shown in life is the excellence that counts.
982.tie_back: The Kural says the only real excellence of the noble is goodness of character and that other excellences do not count, and Guru Nanak likewise ranks truthful living above everything else.
982.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 62, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
982._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); a strong fit on conduct as the supreme good, though the Guru contrasts truthful living with truth itself rather than with beauty, wealth or learning.

983.quote_or_event: “Then were created the five elements and five friends (truth, contentment and compassion etc.) and five enemies (the five evil propensities) of the creatures.”
983.explanation: Bhai Gurdas, the early Sikh exegete, describes creation as setting five virtues in the human being against the five thieves (lust, anger, greed, attachment and ego). Sikh teaching commonly counts the five friends as truth, contentment, compassion, humility and love.
983.tie_back: The Kural rests perfect character on five pillars (love, shame at wrongdoing, generosity, kindliness and truthfulness), and Bhai Gurdas likewise gives the human being five virtues as its support against the five thieves.
983.source: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 39, Pauri 2 (English translation as given on BaniDB/searchgurbani.com)
983._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB; the names of the virtues in parentheses are the translator's gloss, not Bhai Gurdas's own list, and Bhai Gurdas is early exegesis, not scripture, so the five-for-five parallel is suggestive rather than exact.

984.quote_or_event: “It is not good to slander anyone, but the foolish, self-willed manmukhs still do it.”
984.explanation: Guru Amar Das condemns nindaa (speaking ill of others) as the mark of the manmukh, the self-willed person turned away from the Guru. Gurbani often treats slander as a serious spiritual fault.
984.tie_back: The second line of the Kural grounds perfection in not speaking of others' faults, and Guru Amar Das likewise counts refusing to slander as part of a good life.
984.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 755, Raag Suhi, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
984._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); this matches only the Kural's second line, since Sikhism does not treat non-killing as the basis of austerity, rejects austerities as a path, and Sikhs differ among themselves on meat.

985.quote_or_event: “Humility is my spiked club. My dagger is to be the dust of all men’s feet. No evil-doer can withstand these weapons.”
985.explanation: Guru Arjan calls humility his weapon: the club and dagger of the Gurmukh are lowliness and being the dust of everyone's feet, and no evil-doer can stand against them.
985.tie_back: The Kural calls humility the strength of the capable and the weapon by which the noble turn enemies from enmity, and Guru Arjan gives the very same image of humility as an unbeatable weapon.
985.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 628, Raag Sorath, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
985._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on srigranth.org; a near one-to-one match, with humility literally described as a weapon that overcomes opponents.

986.quote_or_event: “If you are wise, be simple; if you are powerful, be weak; and when there is nothing to share, then share with others. How rare is one who is known as such a devotee.”
986.explanation: These saloks ask the strong to choose weakness and the wise to choose simplicity, giving up the advantage they could press. A neighbouring salok of Farid (salok 7, Ang 1378) asks the devotee not to strike back but to kiss the feet of those who strike.
986.tie_back: The Kural makes the willingness to accept defeat even from those beneath one the touchstone of perfection, and Farid's counsel that the powerful should be weak describes that same chosen yielding.
986.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Saloks of Sheikh Farid, salok 128 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
986._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on srigranth.org; a strong thematic fit on the strong choosing to yield, though Farid does not frame it, as the Kural does, as a test or touchstone of character.

987.quote_or_event: “Fareed, answer evil with goodness; do not fill your mind with anger.”
987.explanation: Sheikh Farid's salok, kept in the Guru Granth Sahib, tells the devotee to return good for evil and not to let anger take hold. Sikh tradition honours the same ideal in Bhai Kanhaiya, who gave water to the wounded of both sides.
987.tie_back: The Kural asks what perfection is worth if it will not do kindness even to those who have done harm, and Farid's command to answer evil with goodness is that same demand.
987.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1381, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
987._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); a near one-to-one match on doing good to wrongdoers (the Bhai Kanhaiya mention is background only and was not separately verified).

988.quote_or_event: “No one respects the poor man. ... Says Kabir, he alone is poor, who does not have the Naam, the Name of the Lord, in his heart.”
988.explanation: Kabir begins by describing how the world despises the poor and fawns on the rich. He ends by turning the word around: the only real poverty is to lack the Name of God within.
988.tie_back: The Kural says poverty is no disgrace to one who has the inner strength of perfect character, and Kabir likewise denies that poverty of goods is real poverty for someone inwardly rich.
988.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1159, Raag Bhairao, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
988._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on srigranth.org (the ellipsis omits the middle verses); a near match, with Kabir's inner wealth being the Naam where the Kural's is perfected character.

989.quote_or_event: “The soul becomes steady, and does not waver, by the natural inclination of the Guru's Loving Will.”
989.explanation: Guru Amar Das describes the Gurmukh whose soul, attuned to the Guru's love, becomes adol, unshakable. Gurbani often praises this steadiness against the swaying of Maya and the five passions.
989.tie_back: The Kural says the ocean-like perfected do not change even when the ages shift, and Guru Amar Das likewise describes a soul made steady so that it does not waver.
989.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 87, Sri Raag, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
989._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); a partial fit, since the verse speaks of inner steadiness through the Guru's love but lacks the Kural's cosmic image of standing firm while the ages dissolve.

990.quote_or_event: “The mythical bull is Dharma, the son of compassion; this is what patiently holds the earth in its place. One who understands this becomes truthful. What a great load there is on the bull!”
990.explanation: Guru Nanak takes the old Indian image of a bull holding up the earth and reinterprets it: what really bears the world is dharma, born of compassion. The weight of creation rests on righteousness, not on a literal animal.
990.tie_back: The Kural says the earth could not bear its burden if the noble fell short, and Japji likewise makes moral righteousness the support that keeps the earth in place.
990.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 3, Japji Sahib, Pauri 16, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
990._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on srigranth.org; a strong fit on righteousness bearing the world, though Japji speaks of dharma itself rather than of noble people as the support.
